name: Crinagoras of Mytilene
bio: Crinagoras of Mytilene (c. 70 BC – after AD 11) belonged to the circle of Augustus and Octavia and served as an envoy of his city to Rome. He is among the main poets of the Garland of Philippus.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poems.title: Book V, 108: Epitaph on a lady called Prote
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Unhappy! what first shall I say, what last? Unhappy! that is the essence of all woe. Thou - art gone, O lovely lady, excelling in the beauty of thy body, in the sweetness of thy soul. Rightly they named thee Prote (First): for all was second to the peerless charm that was thine.

poems.title: Book V, 119
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Crinagoras, though thou tossest now to the left, now to the right on thy empty bed, unless lovely Gemella lie by thee, thy rest will bring thee no sleep, but only weariness.

poems.title: Book VI, 100
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Antiphanes, whose father bore the same name, dedicated® to Hermes, still burning in his hand, the torch, object of the young men’s holy strife, the glorious meed of victory, having run swiftly with it, as if mindful of how Prometheus stole the fire.

poems.title: Book VI, 161
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Marcellus, returning from the western war, laden with spoil, to the boundaries of rocky Italy, first shaved his yellow beard. Such was his country’s wish, to send him forth a boy and receive him back a man. singing is the rhythmical tapping of it against the loom by the worker.

poems.title: Book VI, 227
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: This silver pen-nib, with its newly polished holder, nicely moulded with two easily dividing tips, running glib with even flow over the rapidly written page, Crinagoras sends you, Proclus, for your birthday, a little token of great affection, which will sympathize with your newly acquired readiness in learning.t which, though not, I think, right, gives the required sense.

poems.title: Book VI, 229
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: This quill of a crooked-beaked eagle, sharpened to a point by the steel and dyed with purple lacquer, which skilfully removes with its gentle pick any fragments that may be concealed in the teeth after dinner, Crinagoras, your devoted friend, sends you, Lucius, a little token of no small affection, just a mere convivial gift.

poems.title: Book VI, 232
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Philoxenides offers a modest feast to Pan with the sheperd’s crook, and Priapus with the beautiful horns. There are grapes ripe for wine-making, and fragments of the pomegranate easily split, and the yellow marrow of the pine cone, and almonds afraid of being cracked, and the bees’ ambrosia, and short-cakes of sesame, and relishing heads of garlic and pears with shining pips, (?) abundant little diversions for the stomach of the wine-drinker.

poems.title: Book VI, 242
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: On the long-desired morn we offer this sacrifice to Zeus Teleius and Artemis who soothes the pangs of child-bed. For to them did my brother while yet beardless vow to offer the first spring-bloom that clothes the cheeks of young men. Accept it, ye gods, and from this season of his tender beard lead Eucleides straight on to the season of grey hairs.

poems.title: Book VI, 244
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Hera, mother of the Ilithyiae, and thou, Hera Perfectress, and Zeus, the common father of all who are born, hear my prayer and grant that gentle pangs may come to Antonia? in the tender hands of Hepione, so that her husband may rejoice and her mother and her mother-in-law. Her womb bears the blood of great houses.

poems.title: Book VI, 253
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Caves of the Nymphs with many springs, from which such abundance of water trickles down this winding slope; and thou, echoing shrine of Pan crowned with pine-leaves, the home that is his at the foot of the woodland rock; ye stumps of the ancient juniper, holy to hunters, and thou, stone-heap raised in Hermes’ honour, be gracious unto us and accept the spoil of fortunate Sosander’s swift chase of the deer.

poems.title: Book VI, 261
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Son of Simon, since this is your birthday, Crinagoras sends me with the rejoicings of his heart as a gift to the house of his sweetest friend. I am a bronze flask, just like silver, of Indian workmanship

poems.title: Book VI, 345
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Roses used to flower in spring, but we now in mid-winter burst scarlet from our buds, smiling gaily on this thy natal morn that falls so nigh to thy wedding. To be seen on the brow of the loveliest of women is better than to await the sun of spring.

poems.title: Book VI, 350: To a Trumpet
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The Tyrrhenian trumpet that often over the plain of Pisa hath uttered shrilly its piercing note, past time did limit to two prizes. But for that thou hast led Demosthenes of Miletus to three victories, no brazen bell shall ever peal with fuller tone than thine.

poems.title: Book VII, 371
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Earth was my mother’s name, and earth too covers me now I am dead. No worse is this earth than the other: in this I shall lie for long, but from my mother the violent heat of the sun snatched me away and in a strange earth I lie under a stone, Inachus, the much bewept and the obedient servant of Crinagoras.

poems.title: Book VII, 376
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Unhappy men why do we wander confiding in empty hopes, oblivious of painful death? Here was this Seleucus so perfect in speech and character; but after enjoying his prime but for a season, in Spain, at the end of the world, so far from Lesbos, he lies a stranger on that uncharted coast.

poems.title: Book VII, 380
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Though the monument be of Parian marble, and polished by the mason’s straight rule, itis not a good man’s. Do not, good sir, estimate the dead by the stone. The stone is senseless and can cover a foul black corpse as well as any other. Here lies that weak rag the body of Eunicides and rots under the ashes.

poems.title: Book VII, 401
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The tomb above his odious head crushes the bones of the scoundrel who lies in this unhappy earth; it crushes the protruding breast and the unsavoury sawlike teeth and the servilely fettered legs and hairless head, the half consumed remains of Eunicides still full of green putrescence. O earth, who hast espoused an evil bridegroom, rest not light or thinly-sprinkled on the ashes of the deformed being.

poems.title: Book VII, 628
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Other islands ere this have rejected their inglorious names and named themselves after men. Be called Erotides (Love islands), ye Oxeiai (Sharp islands); it is no shame for you to change; for Eros himself gave both his name and his beauty to the boy whom Dies laid here beneath a heap of clods. O earth, crowded with tombs, and sea that washest on the shore, do thou lie light on the boy, and thou lie hushed for his sake.

poems.title: Book VII, 633
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The moon herself, rising at early eve, dimmed her light, veiling her mourning in night, because she saw her namesake, pretty Selene, going down dead to murky Hades, On her she had bestowed the beauty of her light, and with her death she mingled her own darkness.

poems.title: Book VII, 636
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: O happy shepherd, would that I, too, had led my sheep down this grassy white knoll, answering the bleatings of the rams that lead the flock, rather than dipped in the bitter brine the rudder to guide my ship. Therefore I sunk to the depths, and the whistling east wind brought me to rest on this beach.

poems.title: Book VII, 638
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The poor mother, when the expected fate of her two sons was reversed, spoke thus, clasping both of them: “Neither did I hope, my child, to weep for thee to-day, nor, my child, to see thee yet among the living. Now your fates have been interchanged, but sorrow undeniable has come to me.”

poems.title: Book VII, 643
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: O Hades the inexorable, thou hast carried off Hymnis, Evander’s daughter, ever the loveable pet of his house, the coaxing nine-year old girl. Why didst thou send such early death to her who must one day in any case be thine?

poems.title: Book VII, 645
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: O Philostratus, unhappy for all thy wealth, where are those sceptres and constant intercourse with princes on which thy fortune ever depended? Shall thy tomb be (?) by the Nile conspicuous in the region of . . .? Foreigners have shared among them the fruit of thy toil, and thy corpse shall lie in sandy Ostracine.

poems.title: Book VII, 741
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Cite Othryadas, the great glory of Sparta, or Cynegeirus, the sea-fighter, or all great deeds of arms. The Italian warrior who lay by the streams of the Rhine, half dead from many wounds, when he saw the eagle of his dear legion seized by the enemy, again arose from amid the corpses of the slain and killing him who carried it, recovered it for his leaders, alone winning for himself a death that knew not defeat.

poems.title: Book IX, 81
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Tell me not that death is the end of life. The dead, like the living, have their own causes of suffering. Look at the fate of Nicias of Cos... He had gone to rest in Hades, and now his dead body has come again into the light of day. For his fellow-citizens, forcing the bolts of his tomb, dragged out the poor hard-dying ? wretch to punishment.

poems.title: Book IX, 224
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: I am the good milch-goat with udders yielding more than any the milk-pan ever drained, and Caesar, when he had tasted the richness of my milk, sweet as honey, took me with him even on the ship to be his fellow-voyager. Some day I think I shall even reach the stars, for he to whom I gave suck from my breast is by no means inferior to the Aegis-bearer.

poems.title: Book IX, 234
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: How long, wretched soul, upborne by empty hopes nigh to the cold clouds, shalt thou build thee dream upon dream of wealth? Naught falls of its own accord into the possession of man. Pursue the gifts of the Muses, and leave these dim phantoms of the mind to fools.

poems.title: Book IX, 235: On the marriage of Cleopatra (daughter of Antony and Cleopatra) with Juba, King of Numidia
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Great bordering regions of the world which the full stream of Nile separates from the black Aethiopians, ye have by marriage made your sovereigns common to both, turning Egypt and Libya into one country. May the children of these princes ever again rule with unshaken dominion over both lands.

poems.title: Book IX, 239
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The sweet company of the five lyric poets united in this volume offer the work of the inimitable Graces. We come on her festal morning to Antonia, supreme in beauty and mind,

poems.title: Book IX, 276
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The serving-woman washing clothes on the sea-beach, a little above the wet rocks, was swept off, poor wretch, by a breaker which flooded the shore, and she drunk the bitter wave of death. She was in one moment released from life and from poverty. Who in a ship shall brave that sea from which even those on land are not protected ?

poems.title: Book IX, 283
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Ye Pyrenees and ye deep-valleyed Alps that look down from nigh on the sources of the Rhine, ye are witnesses of the lightning that Germanicus flashes forth as he smites the Celts with the thunderbolts of war. In masses the foe fell, and Enyo said to Ares, “Tt is to such hands as these that our help is due.”

poems.title: Book IX, 284
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: What inhabitants, O luckless city, hast thou received, and in place of whom? Alas for the great calamity to Greece! Would, Corinth, thou didst lie lower than the ground and more desert than the Libyan sands, rather than that wholly abandoned to such a crowd of scoundrelly slaves, thou shouldst vex the bones of the ancient Bacchiadae!

poems.title: Book IX, 291: Written after a reverse of the Roman arms in Germany
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Nor though Ocean arouses all his floods, not though Germany drinks up the whole Rhine, shall the might of Rome be shaken as long as she remains confident in Caesar’s auspicious guidance. So the holy oaks of Zeus stand firm on their roots, but the wind strips them of the withered leaves.

poems.title: Book IX, 419
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: With most august Caesar, even if he go to the depths of the Hercynian forest or to extreme Soloeis ! and the western edge of Libya, goeth everywhere glory. The waters of the Pyrenees testify it. They in which not even the neighbouring wood-cutters washed, shall now be baths for two continents.

poems.title: Book IX, 429
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Aristo sung of Nauplius, the watchman of sea-beaten Euboea, and the song set me on fire, valiant as I am. The flame of that false beacon shown in the night from the rock of Caphereus caught my ill-fated heart.

poems.title: Book IX, 430
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: This sheep is a native of Agarra, where the feltcapped Armenians drink the water of Araxes. Its fleece is not, like a sheep’s, composed of soft wool, but thin-haired and rougher than a wild goat’s. Every year it bears triplets, and the teats of its udders are always full of milk. Its bleating resembles most the lowing of a tender calf, for diverse lands bear all things different.

poems.title: Book IX, 439: On a Skull
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Once hairy crown, deserted shell of the eye, fabric of the tongueless mouth, feeble fence of the brain, relic of the unburied dead, set by the wayside to draw a tear from passers-by, thou liest there by the path near the tree-trunk, that looking on thee we may learn what profit there is in being thrifty of life.

poems.title: Book IX, 513: On an Actor
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Thou didst excel in the many dramas that Menander, with one of the Muses or one of the Graces, wrote. ;

poems.title: Book IX, 516
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: “Let every man ply his own trade,” indeed. Under the high Alps the shock-headed robbers, when they have a job in hand, thus avoid the watch-dogs. They grease themselves thickly with kidney-fat to deceive the dogs’ keen scent. It is more ready in devising evil than good, the Ligurian mind.

poems.title: Book IX, 542
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Never fear, Philonides; write a piece composed for four parts or even more ; for neither your singing nor the motions of Bathyllus’ hands shall be lacking in grace.

poems.title: Book IX, 545: With a copy of Callimachus’ Hecale
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: This chiselled poem is Callimachus’, for in it he let out every reef of his Muse. He sings the hut of hospitable Hecale, and all the labours that Marathon imposed on Theseus. May the young strength of Theseus’ hands be thine, Marcellus, and a life of equal renown.

poems.title: Book IX, 555: On the Island of Sybota
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: I am an island, small, seven stadia long, though the geographers neglected (?) to measure me; but still you will see that when I am ploughed I give birth to fat crops, and that I am rich in every kind of fruit, and have plenty of fish to catch, and cool breezes in the dog-days, and the gentleness of unruffed harbours. I am near Phaeacian Coreyra. So that I might be made fun of, I took this name of which I am highly proud.

poems.title: Book IX, 559
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: I am getting ready to sail to Italy, for I am on my way to my friends from whom I have been absent for so long. I am in search of a navigator to conduct me and bring me to the Cyclades and ancient Corcyra. But I beg for your help too, my friend Menippus, author of the learned circular tour! and versed in all geography.

poems.title: Book IX, 560
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Earthquake, most dread of all shocks, whether thou art aroused by the upshaken currents of the sea or of the winds, spare my new-built house, for I know not yet any terror to equal the quivering of the earth.

poems.title: Book IX, 562
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The parrot that talks with human voice, taking leave of his wicker cage, flew to the woods on his many-coloured wings, and ever assiduous in greeting famous Caesar, did not forget that name even in the mountains. All the birds, sharpening their wits to learn, strove among each other which should be the first to say “Chaire”! to the god. Orpheus made the beasts obey him in the hills, and now every bird tunes its voice for thee, Caesar, unbidden.

poems.title: Book X, 24
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Holy spirit of the mighty Earth-shaker, be gracious to others, too, who cross the #gean brine. For to me, driven swiftly by the Thracian breeze,’ gently hast thou granted the harbour I was fain to reach.

poems.title: Book XI, 42
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Though thy life be always sedentary, and thou hast never sailed on the sea or traversed the high roads of the land, yet set thy foot on the Attic soil, that thou mayest see those long nights of Demeter’s holy rites, whereby while thou art among the living thy mind shall be free from care, and “when thou goest to join the greater number it shall be lighter.

poems.title: Book XVI, 40
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Not only three Fortunes should be thy neighbours, Crispus, because of the great riches of thy heart, but all the fortunes of all the world; for to so great a man what honour shall suffice for his infinite benevolence to his friends? But now may Caesar, who is even more powerful than these Fortunes, raise thee to higher dignities. What fortune stands firm without him?

poems.title: Book XVI, 61
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: East and West are the limits of the world, and through both ends of the earth passed the exploits of Nero. The Sun as he rose saw Armenia subdued by his hands and Germany as he went down the sky. Let us sing his double victory in war; Araxes knows it and Rhine, drank now by enslaved peoples.

poems.title: Book XVI, 199: On the Same
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: Weep and moan, thou artful schemer, the sinews of thy hands made fast: thou hast thy desert. None will untie thee; make not those piteous faces; for thou thyself, Love, didst wring the tears from other eyes, and piercing the heart with thy bitter darts, didst instil the venom of desire that takes fast hold. The woes of mortals are thy sport. Thou hast suffered what thou hast done. An excellent thing is justice.

poems.title: Book XVI, 273: On a Picture of the Physician Praxagoras
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text: The son of Phoebus himself, anointing his hand with juice of the all-healing herb, rubbed into thy breast, Praxagoras, the pain-stilling science of medicine. Therefore thou knowest from gentle Hepione herself all woes that spring from long fevers, and what drugs it is fitting to lay on flesh cut by the knife. Had mortals had sufficient of such healers, the boat heavy with the dead would never have crossed the ferry.

poems.title: To the God of the Sea (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Holy Spirit of the great Shaker of Earth, be thou gracious to others also who ply across the Aegean brine; since even to me, chased by the Thracian hurricane, thou didst open out the calm haven of my desire.

poems.title: To the Gods of the Chase (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Fountained caverns of the Nymphs that drip so much water down this jagged headland, and echoing hut of pine-coronalled Pan, wherein he dwells under the feet of the rock of Bassae, and stumps of aged juniper sacred among hunters, and stone-heaped seat of Hermes, be gracious and receive the spoils of the swift stag-chase from Sosander prosperous in hunting.

poems.title: The Great Mysteries (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Though thy life be fixed in one seat, and thou sailest not the sea nor treadest the roads on dry land, yet by all means go to Attica that thou mayest see those great nights of the worship of Demeter; whereby thou shalt possess thy soul without care among the living, and lighter when thou must go to the place that awaiteth all.

poems.title: A Rose in Winter (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Roses were now bloomed in spring, but now in midwinter we have opened our crimson cups, smiling in delight on this thy birthday morning, that brings thee so nigh the bridal bed: better for us to be wreathed on the brows of so fair a woman than wait for the spring sun.

poems.title: At the World's End (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Alas, why wander we, trusting in vain hopes and forgetting baneful death? this Seleucus was perfect in his words and ways, but, having enjoyed his youth but a little, among the utmost Iberians, so far away from Lesbos, he lies a stranger on unmapped shores.

poems.title: Telluris Amor (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O happy shepherd, would that even I had shepherded on the mountain along this white grassy hill, making the bleating folk move after the leader rams, rather than have dipped a ship's steering-rudders in the bitter brine: so I sank under the depths, and the east wind that swallowed me down cast me up again on this shore.

poems.title: Sanctissima Coniunx (Mackail)
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Unhappy, by what first word, by what second shall I name thee? unhappy! this word is true in every ill. Thou art gone, O gracious wife, who didst carry off the palm in bloom of beauty and in bearing of soul; Prote wert thou truly called, for all else comes second to those inimitable graces of thine.

poems.title: Roses in Winter
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
In spring it was we roses
  Were used to bloom of old,
Who now in midmost winter
  Our crimson cells unfold,
To greet thee on the birthday
  That shall thy bridal bring.
'Tis more to grace so fair a brow
  Than know the suns of spring.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.108: δειλαίη, τί σε πρῶτον ἔπος, τί δὲ δεύτατον εἴπω;
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
δειλαίη, τί σε πρῶτον ἔπος, τί δὲ δεύτατον εἴπω;
δειλαίη· τοῦτʼ ἐν παντὶ κακῷ ἔτυμον.
οἴχεαι, ὦ χαρίεσσα γύναι, καὶ ἐς εἴδεος ὥρην
ἄκρα καὶ εἰς ψυχῆς ἦθος ἐνεγκαμένη.
πρώτη σοι ὄνομʼ ἔσκεν ἐτήτυμον ἦν γὰρ ἅπαντα
δεύτερʼ ἀμιμήτων τῶν ἐπὶ σοὶ χαρίτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.119: κἢν ῥίψῃς ἐπὶ λαιά, καὶ ἢν ἐπὶ δεξιὰ ῥίψῃς,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
κἢν ῥίψῃς ἐπὶ λαιά, καὶ ἢν ἐπὶ δεξιὰ ῥίψῃς,
Κριναγόρη, κενεοῦ σαυτὸν ὕπερθε λέχους,
εἰ μή σοι χαρίεσσα παρακλίνοιτο Γέμελλα,
γνώσῃ κοιμηθεὶς οὐχ ὕπνον, ἀλλὰ κόπον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.100: λαμπάδα, τὴν κούροις ἱερὴν ἔριν, ὠκὺς ἐνέγκας,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
λαμπάδα, τὴν κούροις ἱερὴν ἔριν, ὠκὺς ἐνέγκας,
οἷα Προμηθείης μνῆμα πυροκλοπίης,
νίκης κλεινὸν ἄεθλον, ἔτʼ ἐκ χερὸς ἔμπυρον Ἑρμῇ
θῆκεν † ὁμωνυμίῃ παῖς πατρὸς Ἀντιφάνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.161: ἑσπερίου Μάρκελλος ἀνερχόμενος πολέμοιο
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἑσπερίου Μάρκελλος ἀνερχόμενος πολέμοιο
σκυλοφόρος κραναῆς τέλσα παρʼ Ἰταλίης,
ξανθὴν πρῶτον ἔκειρε γενειάδα· βούλετο πατρὶς
οὕτως, καὶ πέμψαι παῖδα καὶ ἄνδρα λαβεῖν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.227: ἀργύρεόν σοι τόνδε, γενέθλιον ἐς τεὸν ἦμαρ,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἀργύρεόν σοι τόνδε, γενέθλιον ἐς τεὸν ἦμαρ,
Πρόκλε, νεόσμηκτον † δουρατίην κάλαμον,
εὖ μὲν ἐυσχίστοισι διάγλυπτον κεράεσσιν,
εὖ δὲ ταχυνομένην εὔροον εἰς σελίδα,
πέμπει Κριναγόρης, ὀλίγην δόσιν, ἀλλʼ ἀπὸ θυμοῦ
πλείονος, ἀρτιδαεῖ σύμπνοον εὐμαθίῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.229: αἰετοῦ ἀγκυλοχείλου ἀκρόπτερον ὀξὺ σιδήρῳ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
αἰετοῦ ἀγκυλοχείλου ἀκρόπτερον ὀξὺ σιδήρῳ
γλυφθέν, καὶ βαπτῇ πορφύρεον κυάνῳ,
ἤν τι λάθῃ μίμνον μεταδόρπιον ἐντὸς ὀδόντων,
κινῆσαι πρηεῖ κέντρῳ ἐπιστάμενον,
βαιὸν ἀπʼ οὐκ ὀλίγης πέμπει φρενός, οἷα δὲ δαιτὸς
δῶρον, ὁ πᾶς ἐπὶ σοί, Λεύκιε, Κριναγόρης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.232: βότρυες οἰνοπέπαντοι, ἐυσχίστοιό τε ῥοιῆς
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
βότρυες οἰνοπέπαντοι, ἐυσχίστοιό τε ῥοιῆς
θρύμματα, καὶ ξανθοὶ μυελοὶ ἐκ στροβίλων,
καὶ δειλαὶ δάκνεσθαι ἀμυγδάλαι, ἥ τε μελισσῶν
ἀμβροσίη, πυκναὶ τʼ ἰτρινέαι ποπάδες,
καὶ πότιμοι γέλγιθες, ἰδʼ † ὑελακύκαδες ὄγχναι,
δαψιλῆ οἰνοπόταις γαστρὸς ἐπεισόδια·
Πανὶ φιλοσκήπωνι καὶ εὐστόρθυγγι Πριήπῳ
ἀντίθεται λιτὴν δαῖτα Φιλοξενίδης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.242: ἠοῖ ἐπʼ εὐκταίῃ τάδε ῥέζομεν ἱρὰ τελείῳ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἠοῖ ἐπʼ εὐκταίῃ τάδε ῥέζομεν ἱρὰ τελείῳ
Ζηνὶ καὶ ὠδίνων μειλίχῳ Ἀρτέμιδι.
τοῖσι γὰρ οὑμὸς ὅμαιμος ἔτʼ ἄχνοος εὔξατο θήσειν
τὸ πρῶτον γενύων ἠιθέοισιν ἔαρ.
δαίμονες ἀλλὰ δέχοισθε καὶ αὐτίκα τῶνδʼ ἀπʼ ἰούλων
Εὐκλείδην πολιῆς ἄχρις ἄγοιτε τριχός.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.244: Ἥρη, Ἐλειθυιῶν μήτηρ, Ἥρη τε τελείη,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ἥρη, Ἐλειθυιῶν μήτηρ, Ἥρη τε τελείη,
καὶ Ζεῦ, γινομένοις ξυνὸς ἅπασι πατήρ,
ὠδῖνας νεύσαιτʼ Ἀντωνίῃ ἵλαοι ἐλθεῖν
πρηείας, μαλακαῖς χερσὶ σὺν Ἠπιόνης,
ὄφρα κε γηθήσειε πόσις, μήτηρ θʼ, ἑκυρά τε.
ἡ νηδὺς οἴκων αἷμα φέρει μεγάλων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.253: σπήλυγγες Νυμφῶν ἐυπίδακες, αἱ τόσον ὕδωρ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
σπήλυγγες Νυμφῶν ἐυπίδακες, αἱ τόσον ὕδωρ
εἴβουσαι σκολιοῦ τοῦδε κατὰ πρεόνος,
Πανὸς τʼ ἠχήεσσα πιτυστέπτοιο καλιή,
τὴν ὑπὸ βησσαίης ποσσὶ λέλογχε πέτρης,
ἱερὰ τʼ ἀγρευταῖσι γερανδρύου ἀρκεύθοιο
πρέμνα, λιθηλογέες θʼ Ἑρμέω ἱδρύσιες,
αὐταί θʼ ἱλήκοιτε, καὶ εὐθήροιο δέχεσθε
Σωσάνδρου ταχινῆς σκῦλʼ ἐλαφοσσοΐης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.261: χάλκεον ἀργυρέῳ με πανείκελον, Ἰνδικὸν ἔργον,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
χάλκεον ἀργυρέῳ με πανείκελον, Ἰνδικὸν ἔργον,
ὄλπην, ἡδίστου ξείνιον εἰς ἑτάρου,
ἦμαρ ἐπεὶ τόδε σεῖο γενέθλιον, υἱὲ Σίμωνος,
πέμπει γηθομένῃ σὺν φρενὶ Κριναγόρης,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.345: εἴαρος ἤνθει μὲν τὸ πρὶν ῥόδα, νῦν δʼ ἐνὶ μέσσῳ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
εἴαρος ἤνθει μὲν τὸ πρὶν ῥόδα, νῦν δʼ ἐνὶ μέσσῳ
χείματι πορφυρέας ἐσχάσαμεν κάλυκας,
σῇ ἐπιμειδήσαντα γενεθλίῃ ἄσμενα τῇδε
ἠοῖ, νυμφιδίων ἀσσοτάτῃ λεχέων.
καλλίστης ὀφθῆναι ἐπὶ κροτάφοισι γυναικὸς
λώιον ἢ μίμνειν ἠρινὸν ἠέλιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.350: Τυρσηνῆς κελάδημα διαπρύσιον σάλπιγγος,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Τυρσηνῆς κελάδημα διαπρύσιον σάλπιγγος,
πολλάκι Πισαίων στρηνὲς ὑπὲρ πεδίων
φθεγξαμένης, ὁ πρὶν μὲν ἔχει χρόνος ἐν δυσὶ νίκαις·
εἰ δὲ σὺ καὶ τρισσοὺς ἤγαγες εἰς στεφάνους
ἀστὸν Μιλήτου Δημοσθένεʼ, οὔ ποτε κώδων
χάλκεος ἠχήσει πλειοτέρῳ στόματι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.371: γῆ μευ καὶ μήτηρ κικλήσκετο· γῆ με καλύπτει
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
γῆ μευ καὶ μήτηρ κικλήσκετο· γῆ με καλύπτει
καὶ νέκυν. οὐ κείνης ἥδε χερειοτέρη·
ἔσσομαι ἐν ταύτῃ δηρὸν χρόνον ἐκ δέ με μητρὸς
ἥρπασεν ἠελίου καῦμα τὸ θερμότατον.
κεῖμαι δʼ ἐν ξείνῃ, ὑπὸ χερμάδι, μακρὰ γοηθείς,
Ἴναχος, εὐπειθὴς Κριναγόρου θεράπων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.376: δείλαιοι, τί κεναῖσιν ἀλώμεθα θαρσήσαντες
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
δείλαιοι, τί κεναῖσιν ἀλώμεθα θαρσήσαντες
ἐλπίσιν, ἀτηροῦ ληθόμενοι θανάτου;
ἦν ὅδε καὶ μύθοισι καὶ ἤθεσι πάντα Σέλευκος
ἄρτιος, ἀλλʼ ἥβης βαιὸν ἐπαυρόμενος,
ὑστατίοις ἐν Ἴβηρσι, τόσον δίχα τηλόθι Λέσβου,
κεῖται ἀμετρήτων ξεῖνος ἐπʼ αἰγιαλῶν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.380: εἰ καὶ τὸ σῆμα λυγδίνης ἀπὸ πλακὸς
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
εἰ καὶ τὸ σῆμα λυγδίνης ἀπὸ πλακὸς
καὶ ξεστὸν ὀρθῇ λαοτέκτονος στάθμῃ,
οὐκ ἀνδρὸς ἐσθλοῦ. μὴ λίθῳ τεκμαίρεο,
ὦ λῷστε, τὸν θανόντα. κωφὸν ἡ λίθος,
τῇ καὶ ζοφώδης ἀμφιέννυται νέκυς.
κεῖται δὲ τῇδε τὠλιγηπελὲς ῥάκος
Εὐνικίδαο, σήπεται δʼ ὑπὸ σποδῷ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.401: τήνδʼ ὑπὸ δύσβωλον θλίβει χθόνα φωτὸς ἀλιτροῦ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
τήνδʼ ὑπὸ δύσβωλον θλίβει χθόνα φωτὸς ἀλιτροῦ
ὀστέα μισητῆς τύμβος ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς,
στέρνα τʼ ἐποκριόεντα, καὶ οὐκ εὔοδμον ὀδόντων
πρίονα, καὶ κώλων δούλιον οἰοπέδην,
ἄτριχα καὶ κόρσην, Εὐνικίδου ἡμιπύρωτα
λείψανʼ, ἔτι χλωρῆς ἔμπλεα τηκεδόνος.
χθὼν ὦ δυσνύμφευτε, κακοσκήνευς ἐπὶ τέφρης
ἀνδρὸς μὴ κούφη κέκλισο, μηδʼ ὀλίγη,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.628: ἠρνήσαντο καὶ ἄλλαι ἑὸν πάρος οὔνομα νῆσοι
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἠρνήσαντο καὶ ἄλλαι ἑὸν πάρος οὔνομα νῆσοι
ἀκλεές, ἐς δʼ ἀνδρῶν ἦλθον ὁμωνυμίην·
κληθείητε καὶ ὔμμες Ἐρωτίδες· οὐ νέμεσίς τοι,
ὀξεῖαι, ταύτην κλῆσιν ἀμειψαμέναις.
παιδὶ γάρ, ὃν τύμβῳ Δίης ὑπεθήκατο βώλου,
οὔνομα καὶ μορφὴν αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν Ἔρως.
ὦ χθὼν σηματόεσσα, καὶ ἡ παρὰ θινὶ θάλασσα,
παιδὶ σὺ μὲν κούφη κεῖσο, σὺ δʼ ἡσυχίη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.633: καὶ αὐτὴ ἤχλυσεν ἀκρέσπερος ἀντέλλουσα
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
καὶ αὐτὴ ἤχλυσεν ἀκρέσπερος ἀντέλλουσα
μήνη, πένθος ἑὸν νυκτὶ καλυψαμένη,
οὕνεκα τὴν χαρίεσσαν ὁμώνυμον εἶδε Σελήνην
ἄπνουν εἰς ζοφερὸν δυομένην ἀίδην.
κείνῃ γὰρ καὶ κάλλος ἑοῦ κοινώσατο φωτὸς,
καὶ θάνατον κείνης μίξεν ἑῷ κνέφεϊ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.636: ποιμὴν ὦ μάκαρ, εἴθε κατʼ οὔρεος ἐπροβάτευον
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ποιμὴν ὦ μάκαρ, εἴθε κατʼ οὔρεος ἐπροβάτευον
κἠγὼ, ποιηρὸν τοῦτʼ ἀνὰ λευκόλοφον,
κριοῖς ἁγητῆρσι ποτʼ ἐβληχημένα βάζων,
ἢ πικρῇ βάψαι νήοχα πηδάλια
ἅλμῃ. τοιγὰρ ἔδυν ὑποβένθιος· ἀμφὶ δὲ ταύτην
θῖνά με ῥοιβδήσας Εὖρος ἐφωρμίσατο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.638: παίδων ἀλλαχθέντι μόρῳ ἔπι τοῦτʼ ἐλεεινὴ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
παίδων ἀλλαχθέντι μόρῳ ἔπι τοῦτʼ ἐλεεινὴ
μήτηρ ἀμφοτέρους εἶπε περισχομένη·
“ καὶ νέκυν οὐ σέο, τέκνον, ἐπʼ ἤματι τῷδε γοήσειν
ἤλπισα, καὶ ζωοῖς οὐ σὲ μετεσσόμενον.ὄψεσθαι·
νῦν δʼ οἱ μὲν ἐς ὑμέας ἠμείφθησαν
δαίμονες, ἄψευστον δʼ ἵκετο πένθος ἐμοί.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.643: Ὑμνίδα τὴν Εὐάνδρου, ἐράσμιον αἰὲν ἄθυρμα
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ὑμνίδα τὴν Εὐάνδρου, ἐράσμιον αἰὲν ἄθυρμα
οἰκογενές, κούρην αἱμύλον εἰναέτιν,
ἥρπασας, ὦ ἄλλιστʼ Ἀίδη, τί πρόωρον ἐφιεὶς
μοῖραν τῇ πάντως σεῖὸ ποτʼ ἐσσομένῃ;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.645: τί δύστηνʼ ὄλβοιο Φιλόστρατε, ποῦ σοι ἐκεῖνα
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
τί δύστηνʼ ὄλβοιο Φιλόστρατε, ποῦ σοι ἐκεῖνα
σκῆπτρα καὶ αἱ βασιλέων ἄφθονοι ἐντυχίαι,˘
αἷσιν ἐπῃώρησας ἀεὶ βίον; ἦ ἐπὶ Νείλῳ
δαίοις ὢν περίοπτος ὅροις;
ὀθνεῖοι καμάτους τοὺς σοὺς διεμοιρήσαντο,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.741: Ὀθρυάδην, Σπάρτης τὸ μέγα κλέος, ἢ Κυνέγειρον
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ὀθρυάδην, Σπάρτης τὸ μέγα κλέος, ἢ Κυνέγειρον
ναύμαχον, ἢ πάντων ἔργα κάλει πολέμων
Ἄρεος αἰχμητὴς Ἰταλὸς παρὰ χεύμασι Ῥήνου
κλινθείς, ἐκ πολλῶν ἡμιθανὴς βελέων,
αἰετὸν ἁρπασθέντα φίλου στρατοῦ ὡς ἴδʼ ὑπʼ ἐχθροῖς,
αὖτις ἀρηιφάτων ἄνθορεν ἐκ νεκύων
κτείνας δʼ ὃς σφʼ ἐκόμιζεν, ἑοῖς ἀνεσώσατο ταγοῖς,
μοῦνος ἀήττητον δεξάμενος θάνατον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.81: μὴ εἴπῃς θάνατον βιοτῆς ὅρον εἰσὶ καμοῦσιν,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
μὴ εἴπῃς θάνατον βιοτῆς ὅρον εἰσὶ καμοῦσιν,
ὡς ζωοῖς, ἀρχαὶ συμφορέων ἕτεραι.
ἄθρει Νικίεω Κῴου μόρον ἤδη ἔκειτο
εἰν ἀίδῃ, νεκρὸς δʼ ἦλθεν ὑπʼ ἠέλιον
ἀστοὶ γὰρ τύμβοιο μετοχλίσσαντες ὀχῆας,
εἴρυσαν ἐς ποινὰς τλήμονα δυσθανέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.224: αἶγά με τὴν εὔθηλον, ὅσων ἐκένωσεν ἀμολγεὺς
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
αἶγά με τὴν εὔθηλον, ὅσων ἐκένωσεν ἀμολγεὺς
οὔθατα πασάων πουλυγαλακτοτάτην,
γευσάμενος, μελιηδὲς ἐπεὶ τʼ ἐφράσσατο πῖαρ
Καῖσαρ, κἠν νηυσὶν σύμπλοον εἰργάσατο.
ἥξω δʼ αὐτίκα που καὶ ἐς ἀστέρας· ᾧ γὰρ ἐπέσχον
μαζὸν ἐμόν, μείων οὐδʼ ὅσον Αἰγιόχου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.234: ἄχρι τεῦ, ἆ δείλαιε, κεναῖσιν ἐπʼ ἐλπίσι, θυμέ,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἄχρι τεῦ, ἆ δείλαιε, κεναῖσιν ἐπʼ ἐλπίσι, θυμέ,
πωτηθεὶς ψυχρῶν ἀσσοτάτω νεφέων,
ἄλλοις ἄλλʼ ἔπʼ ὄνειρα διαγράψεις ἀφένοιο;
κτητὸν γὰρ θνητοῖς οὐδὲ ἓν αὐτόματον.
Μουσέων ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ δῶρα μετέρχεο· ταῦτα δʼ ἀμυδρὰ
εἴδωλα ψυχῆς ἠλεμάτοισι μέθες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.235: Ἄγχουροι μεγάλαι κόσμου χθόνες, ἃς διὰ Νεῖλος
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ἄγχουροι μεγάλαι κόσμου χθόνες, ἃς διὰ Νεῖλος
πιμπλάμενος μελάνων τέμνει ἀπʼ Αἰθιόπων,
ἀμφότεραι βασιλῆας ἐκοινώσασθε γάμοισιν,
ἓν γένος Αἰγύπτου καὶ Λιβύης θέμεναι.
ἐκ πατέρων εἴη παισὶν πάλι τοῖσιν ἀνάκτων
ἔμπεδον ἠπείροις σκῆπτρον ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέραις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.239: βίβλων ἡ γλυκερὴ λυρικῶν ἐν τεύχεϊ τῷδε
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
βίβλων ἡ γλυκερὴ λυρικῶν ἐν τεύχεϊ τῷδε
πεντὰς ἀμιμήτων ἔργα φέρει Χαρίτων.
δῶρον δʼ εἰς ἱερὴν Ἀντωνίῃ ἥκομεν ἠῶ,
κάλλευς καὶ πραπίδων ἔξοχʼ ἐνεγκαμένῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.276: λῶπος ἀποκλύζουσα παρὰ κροκάλαισι θαλάσσης
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
λῶπος ἀποκλύζουσα παρὰ κροκάλαισι θαλάσσης
χερνῆτις, διεροῦ τυτθὸν ὕπερθε πάγου,
χέρσον ἐπεκβαίνοντι κατασπασθεῖσα κλύδωνι,
δειλαίη πικροῦ κῦμʼ ἔπιεν θανάτου·
πνεῦμα δʼ ὁμοῦ πενίῃ ἀπελύσατο. τίς κʼ ἐνὶ νηὶ
θαρσήσαι πεζοῖς τὴν ἀφύλακτον ἅλα;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.283: οὔρεα Πυρηναῖα καὶ αἱ βαθυάγκεες Ἄλπεις,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
οὔρεα Πυρηναῖα καὶ αἱ βαθυάγκεες Ἄλπεις,
αἳ Ῥήνου προχοὰς ἐγγὺς ἀποβλέπετε,
μάρτυρες ἀκτίνων, Γερμανικὸς ἃς ἀνέτειλεν,
ἀστράπτων Κελτοῖς πουλὺν ἐνυάλιον.
οἱ δʼ ἄρα δουπήθησαν ἀολλέες· εἶπε δʼ Ἐνυὼ
Ἄρεϊ· τοιαύταις χερσὶν ὀφειλόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.284: οἵους ἀνθʼ οἵων οἰκήτορας, ὦ ἐλεεινή,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
οἵους ἀνθʼ οἵων οἰκήτορας, ὦ ἐλεεινή,
εὕραο. φεῦ μεγάλης Ἑλλάδος ἀμμορίης.
αὐτίκα καὶ γαίης χθαμαλωτέρη εἴθε, Κόρινθε,
κεῖσθαι, καὶ Λιβυκῆς ψάμμου ἐρημοτέρη,
ἢ τοίοις διὰ πᾶσα παλιμπρήτοισι δοθεῖσα
θλίβειν ἀρχαίων ὀστέα Βακχιαδῶν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.291: †οὐδʼ ἢν Ὠκεανὸς πᾶσαν πλήμμυραν ἐγείρῃ,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
†οὐδʼ ἢν Ὠκεανὸς πᾶσαν πλήμμυραν ἐγείρῃ,
οὐδʼ ἢν Γερμανίη Ῥῆνον ἅπαντα πίῃ,
Ῥώμης οὐδʼ ὅσσον βλάψει σθένος, ἄχρι κε μίμνῃ
δεξιὰ σημαίνειν Καίσαρι θαρσαλέη.
οὕτως χαἰ ἱεραὶ Ζηνὸς δρύες ἔμπεδα ῥίζαις
ἑστᾶσιν, φύλλων δʼ αὖα χέουσ’ ἄνεμοι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.419: κἢν μυχὸν Ἑρκυναῖον, ἢ ἐς πύματον Σολόεντα
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
κἢν μυχὸν Ἑρκυναῖον, ἢ ἐς πύματον Σολόεντα
ἔλθῃ καὶ Λιβυκῶν κράσπεδον Ἑσπερίδων
Καῖσαρ ὁ πουλυσέβαστος, ἅμα κλέος εἶσιν ἐκείνῳ
πάντῃ. Πυρήνης ὕδατα μαρτύρια·
οἷσι γὰρ οὐδὲ πέριξ δρυτόμοι ἀπεφαιδρύναντο,
λουτρὰ καὶ ἠπείρων ἔσσεται ἀμφοτέρων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.429: τὸν σκοπὸν Εὐβοίης ἁλικύμονος ᾖσεν Ἀριστὼ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
τὸν σκοπὸν Εὐβοίης ἁλικύμονος ᾖσεν Ἀριστὼ
Ναύπλιον ἐκ μολπῆς δʼ ὁ θρασὺς ἐφλεγόμην.
ὁ ψεύστης δʼ ὑπὸ νύκτα Καφηρείης ἀπὸ πέτρης
πυρσὸς ἐμὴν μετέβη δυσμόρον ἐς κραδίην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.430: τῆς ὄιος γενεὴ μὲν Ἀγαρρική, † ἐντὸς Ἀράξεω
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
τῆς ὄιος γενεὴ μὲν Ἀγαρρική, † ἐντὸς Ἀράξεω
ὕδωρ πιλοφόροις πίνεται Ἀρμενίοις·
χαῖται δʼ, οὐ μήλοις ἅτε που μαλακοὶ ἔπι μαλλοί,
ψεδναὶ δʼ, ἀγροτέρων τρηχύτεραι χιμάρων.
νηδὺς δὲ τριτοκεῖ ἀνὰ πᾶν ἔτος, ἐκ δὲ γάλακτος
θηλὴ ἀεὶ μαστοῦ πλήθεται οὐθατίου·
βληχὴ δʼ ἀσσοτάτω τερένης μυκήματι μόσχου·
ἄλλα γὰρ ἀλλοῖαι πάντα φέρουσι γέαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.439: βρέγμα πάλαι λαχναῖον, ἐρημαῖόν τε κέλυφος
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
βρέγμα πάλαι λαχναῖον, ἐρημαῖόν τε κέλυφος
ὄμματος, ἀγλώσσου θʼ ἁρμονίη στόματος,
ψυχῆς ἀσθενὲς ἕρκος., ἀτυμβεύτου θανάτοιο
λείψανον, εἰνόδιον δάκρυ παρερχομένων,
κεῖσο πέλας πρέμνοιο παρʼ ἀτραπόν, ὄφρα μάθῃ τις
ἀθρήσας, τί πλέον φειδομένῳ βιότου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.513: δράμασιν ἐν πολλοῖσι διέπρεπες, ὅσσα Μένανδρος
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
δράμασιν ἐν πολλοῖσι διέπρεπες, ὅσσα Μένανδρος
ἔγραφεν, ἢ Μουσέων σὺν μιῇ ἢ Χαρίτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.516: ἔρδοι τὴν ἔμαθέν τις, ὅπου καὶ ὑπʼ Ἄλπιας ἄκρας
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
ἔρδοι τὴν ἔμαθέν τις, ὅπου καὶ ὑπʼ Ἄλπιας ἄκρας
ληισταὶ λασίαις ἀμφίκομοι κεφαλαῖς,
φωρῆς ἁπτόμενοι, φύλακας κύνας ὧδʼ ἀλέονται
χρίονται νεφροῖς πῖαρ ἔπεστιν ὅσον,
ψευδόμενοι ῥινῶν ὀξὺν στίβον. ὦ κακὸν εὑρεῖν
ῥηΐτεραι Λιγύων μήτιες ἢ ἀγαθόν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.542: θάρσει καὶ τέτταρσι διαπλασθέντα προσώποις
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
θάρσει καὶ τέτταρσι διαπλασθέντα προσώποις
μῦθον καὶ τούτων γράψαι ἔτι πλέοσιν
οὔτε σὲ γὰρ λείψουσι, Φιλωνίδη, οὔτε Βάθυλλον,
τὸν μὲν ἀοιδάων, τὸν δὲ χερῶν χάριτες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.545: Καλλιμάχου τὸ τορευτὸν ἔπος τόδε· δὴ γὰρ ἐπʼ αὐτῷ
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Καλλιμάχου τὸ τορευτὸν ἔπος τόδε· δὴ γὰρ ἐπʼ αὐτῷ
ὡνὴρ τοὺς Μουσέων πάντας ἔσεισε κάλους.
ἀείδει δʼ Ἑκάλης τε φιλοξείνοιο καλιὴν
καὶ Θησεῖ Μαραθὼν οὓς ἐπέθηκε πόνους,
τοῦ σοὶ καὶ νεαρὸν χειρῶν σθένος εἴη ἀρέσθαι,
Μάρκελλε, κλεινοῦ τʼ αἶνον ἴσον βιότου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.555: νῆσον τήν, εἰ καί με περιγράψαντες † ἔχουσιν
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
νῆσον τήν, εἰ καί με περιγράψαντες † ἔχουσιν
μετρῆσαι, βαιήν, ἑπτὰ μόνον σταδίους,
ἔμπης καὶ τίκτουσαν ἐπʼ αὔλακα πῖαρ ἀρότρου
ὄψει, καὶ παντὸς κάρπιμον ἀκροδρύου,
καὶ πολλοῖς εὔαγρον ὑπʼ ἰχθύσι, καὶ ὑπὸ μαίρῃ
εὐάνεμον, λιμένων τʼ ἤπιον ἀτρεμίῃ,
ἀγχόθι Κορκύρης Φαιηκίδος. ἀλλὰ γελᾶσθαι
† τῷ ἔπʼ ἐωρίσθην, τοῦτʼ ἐθέμην ὄνομα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.559: πλοῦς μοι ἐπʼ Ἰταλίην ἐντύνεται· ἐς γὰρ ἑταίρους
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
πλοῦς μοι ἐπʼ Ἰταλίην ἐντύνεται· ἐς γὰρ ἑταίρους
στέλλομαι, ὧν ἤδη δηρὸν ἄπειμι χρόνον.
διφέω δʼ ἡγητῆρα περίπλοον , ὅς μʼ ἐπὶ νήσους
Κυκλάδας, ἀρχαίην τʼ ἄξει ἐπὶ Σχερίην.
σὺν τί μοι ἀλλὰ Μένιππε λάβευ φίλος, ἵστορα κύκλον
γράψας, ὦ πάσης ἴδρι γεωγραφίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.560: Ῥιγηλὴ πασῶν ἔνοσι χθονός, εἴτε σε πόντου,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ῥιγηλὴ πασῶν ἔνοσι χθονός, εἴτε σε πόντου,
εἴτʼ ἀνέμων αἴρει ῥεῦμα τινασσόμενον,
οἰκία μοι ῥύευ νεοτευχέα· δεῖμα γὰρ οὔπω
ἄλλο τόσον γαίης οἶδʼ ἐλελιζομένης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.562: Ψιττακὸς ὁ βροτόγηρυς, ἀφεὶς λυγοτευχέα κύρτον,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ψιττακὸς ὁ βροτόγηρυς, ἀφεὶς λυγοτευχέα κύρτον,
ἤλυθεν ἐς δρυμοὺς ἀνθοφυεῖ πτέρυγι.
αἰεὶ δʼ ἐκμελετῶν ἀσπάσμασι Καίσαρα κλεινόν,
οὐδʼ ἀνʼ ὄρη λήθην ἤγαγεν οὐνόματος·
† ἔδραμε δʼ ὠκυδίδακτος ἅπας οἰωνός, βρίζων
τίς φθῆναι δύναται δαίμονι χαῖρʼ ἐνέπειν.
Ὀρφεὺς θῆρας ἔπεισεν ἐν οὔρεσι· καὶ δὲ σέ, Καῖσαρ,
νῦν ἀκέλευστος ἅπας ὄρνις ἀνακρέκεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.24: φρὴν ἱερὴ μεγάλου Ἐνοσίχθονος, ἔσσο καὶ ἄλλοις
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
φρὴν ἱερὴ μεγάλου Ἐνοσίχθονος, ἔσσο καὶ ἄλλοις
ἠπίη, Αἰγαίην οἳ διέπουσιν ἅλα·
κἠμοὶ γὰρ Θρήικι διωκομένῳ ὑπʼ ἀήτῃ
ὤρεξας πρηεῖʼ ἀσπασίῳ λιμένας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.42: εἰ καί σοι ἑδραῖος ἀεὶ βίος, οὐδὲ θάλασσαν
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
εἰ καί σοι ἑδραῖος ἀεὶ βίος, οὐδὲ θάλασσαν
ἔπλως, χερσαίας τʼ οὐκ ἐπάτησας ὁδούς,
ἔμπης Κεκροπίης ἐπιβήμεναι, ὄφρʼ ἂν,ἐκείνας
Δήμητρος μεγάλας νύκτας ἴδῃς ἱερῶν,
τῶν ἄπο κἠν ζωοῖσιν ἀκηδέα, κεὖτʼ ἂν ἵκηαι
ἐς πλεόνων, ἕξεις θυμὸν ἐλαφρότερον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.40: γείτονες οὐ Τρισσαὶ μοῦνον Τύχαι ἔπρεπον εἶναι,
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.61: Ἀντολίαι, δύσιες, κόσμου μέτρα· καὶ τὰ Νέρωνος
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
Ἀντολίαι, δύσιες, κόσμου μέτρα· καὶ τὰ Νέρωνος
ἔργα διʼ ἀμφοτέρων ἵκετο γῆς περάτων.
ἥλιος Ἀρμενίην ἀνιὼν ὑπὸ χερσὶ δαμεῖσαν
κείνου, Γερμανίην δʼ εἶδε κατερχόμενος.
δισσὸν ἀειδέσθω πολέμου κράτος· οἶδεν Ἀράξης
καὶ Ῥῆνος, δούλοις ἔθνεσι πινόμενοι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.199: καὶ κλαῖε καὶ στέναζε, συσφιγχθεὶς χεροῖν
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
καὶ κλαῖε καὶ στέναζε, συσφιγχθεὶς χεροῖν
τένοντας, ὦ ʼπίβουλε· τοῖά τοι πρέπει.
οὐκ ἔσθʼ ὁ λύσων μὴ λεείνʼ ὑπόβλεπε.
αὐτὸς γὰρ ἄλλων ἐκ μὲν ὀμμάτων δάκρυ
ἔθλιψας, ἐν δὲ πικρὰ καρδίᾳ βέλη
πήξας ἀφύκτων ἰὸν ἔσταξας πόθων,
ἔρως· τὰ θνητῶν δʼ ἐστί σοι γέλως ἄχη
πέπονθας οἷʼ ἔρεξας. ἐσθλὸν ἡ δίκη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.273: αὐτός σοι Φοίβοιο πάις λαθικηδέα τέχνης
poems.author: Crinagoras of Mytilene
poems.text:
αὐτός σοι Φοίβοιο πάις λαθικηδέα τέχνης
ἰδμοσύνην, πανάκῃ χεῖρα λιπηνάμενος,
Πρηξαγόρη, στέρνοις ἐνεμάξατο. τοιγὰρ ἀνῖαι
ὄρνυνται δολιχῶν ὁππόσαι ἐκ πυρετῶν,
καὶ ὁπόσα τμηθέντος ἐπὶ χροὸς ἄρκια θεῖναι
φάρμακα, πρηείης οἶσθα παρʼ Ἠπιόνης.
θνητοῖσιν δʼ εἰ τοῖοι ἐπήρκεον ἰητῆρες,
οὐκ ἂν ἐπορθμεύθη νεκροβαρὴς ἄκατος.
